name: Interview probability, set 3
description: Probability questions of the kind interviewers ask. Topics: order statistics, coupons, patterns, hats, Bayes, ruin, races, Kelly, hedging, doubling, chords, distances and needles. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: Roll three fair six-sided dice. You are paid the middle face in pounds. With 2, 5 and 5 the middle face is 5.
items.question: What is the fair value of the game, in pounds?

widget.accept: £3.50: by symmetry the middle face averages 3.5.
widget.label: Fair value in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what happens to the middle face when each face x becomes 7 − x.

byKey.largest: You priced the largest face, 119/24. The middle face sits between the largest and the smallest.
byKey.smallest: You priced the smallest face, 49/24. The middle face is above it on average.
byKey.uniform: You treated the die as uniform on 0 to 6. Its faces run from 1 to 6, centred on 3.5.

explain.text: Turning each face x into 7 − x keeps the dice fair and turns the middle face m into 7 − m. So the middle face averages the same as 7 minus itself, which forces 3.5. Listing all 216 rolls gives 756/216 = £3.50.

items.prose: A sticker album has 9 different stickers. Each pack holds one sticker, equally likely to be any of the 9, independently of other packs.
items.question: How many packs do you expect to buy to fill the album? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the wait into stages, one per new sticker, and add the geometric waits.

byKey.one-each: You allowed one pack per sticker. Near the end most packs bring a sticker you already have.
byKey.squared: You squared the number of stickers. The wait is 9 times $1 + \tfrac12 + \cdots + \tfrac19$, not 9 times 9.
byKey.no-last: You stopped before the last sticker. It alone takes 9 packs on average, since each pack has a 1 in 9 chance.

explain.text: With k stickers held, a pack is new with chance (9 − k)/9, so that stage takes 9/(9 − k) packs. Adding the stages gives $9(1 + \tfrac12 + \cdots + \tfrac19) = 7129/280 \approx 25.46$. The last sticker alone takes 9 packs, over a third of the total.

items.prose: A trading signal fires on any day with chance 3%, independently of every other day. You watch it for 60 days.
items.question: What is the chance it fires at least once? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance of no fire at all, then take the complement.

byKey.added: You added 60 chances of 3%. Chances of overlapping events do not add, and a chance cannot pass 1.
byKey.none: That is the chance it never fires. Take it from 1.
byKey.poisson: You used the shortcut $1 - e^{-1.8}$. It is close, but the exact chance uses $0.97^{60}$.

explain.text: The signal stays quiet on a day with chance 0.97, so on all 60 days with chance $0.97^{60} \approx 0.1608$. At least one fire is the complement: $1 - 0.1608 = 0.8392$. A seeded simulation of 100,000 runs agrees.

items.prose: Twelve guests leave their coats at a party. At home time the coats come back in a random order, one to each guest. Let X be the number who get their own coat.
items.question: Which pair gives $E[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$?

options.why: You treated the matches as independent, as in a binomial. Two guests both match with chance 1/132, above 1/144, so they are linked.
That is one guest on their own. X adds the twelve guests together.
You gave $E[X^2]$, which is 2. Subtract $(E[X])^2 = 1$ to get the variance.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write X as a sum of indicators, then use pairs of them for $E[X^2]$.

explain.text: Each guest gets their own coat with chance 1/12, so $E[X] = 12 \times \tfrac{1}{12} = 1$. The 132 ordered pairs of guests each both match with chance 1/132, so $E[X^2] = 1 + 1 = 2$. Then $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 2 - 1^2 = 1$, for any number of guests above one.

items.prose: A strategy loses on any day with chance 0.4, independently of other days. Its risk limit stops it after three losing days in a row.
items.question: How many trading days do you expect until the limit stops it? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the current run of losses, 0, 1 or 2, and write a first-step equation for each.

byKey.two-days: You waited for two losing days in a row. The limit needs a third.
byKey.cube: You used $1/0.4^3$, as if each try were three fresh days. A win restarts the run, so the wait is longer.
byKey.per-loss: You allowed 2.5 days per loss, three times. A win between losses resets the run, so that is too short.

explain.text: Let $E_j$ be the expected days left after a run of $j$ losses: $E_j = 1 + 0.4E_{j+1} + 0.6E_0$, with $E_3 = 0$. Solving gives $E_0 = (1 + 0.4 + 0.16)/0.064 = 195/8 = 24.375$. A seeded simulation of 100,000 runs agrees.

items.prose: A signal fires on 55% of good days and on 25% of bad days. Good days make up 30% of all days.
items.question: The signal fires today. What is the chance today is a good day? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Picture 1,000 days and count the firing days of each kind.

byKey.no-base: You compared 55% with 25% and ignored that good days are only 30%. Weight each rate by how common its days are.
byKey.hit-rate: That is the chance of a fire on a good day. You need the reverse: a good day given a fire.
byKey.base-rate: You kept the base rate. A fire is more likely on good days, so it must move the chance up.

explain.text: In 1,000 days, 300 are good and 165 of them fire; 700 are bad and 175 of them fire. The good share of the 340 firing days is $165/340 = 33/68 \approx 0.4853$. Even after a fire, a good day is slightly less likely than a bad one.

items.prose: You hold £3 and bet £1 at a time. Each bet wins with chance 0.45. You stop when you reach £9 or go broke.
items.question: What is the chance you reach £9? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the ruin formula with $r = q/p$.

byKey.fair: You used the fair-game answer, 3/9. At 0.45 each bet drifts against you, so the chance is lower.
byKey.flipped: You used $r = p/q$, which gives the chance for a player who wins 0.55 of bets. Use $r = q/p = 11/9$.
byKey.six-wins: You needed six wins in a row. Losses can be won back, so many other paths reach £9 too.

explain.text: With $r = q/p = 0.55/0.45 = 11/9$, the chance of reaching £9 from £3 is $\dfrac{1 - r^3}{1 - r^9}$. That is $(1 - 1.8258)/(1 - 6.0863) \approx 0.1624$. A small edge against you halves the fair chance of 1/3.

items.prose: Flip a fair coin until HTT or TTH appears. The first of the two patterns to appear wins.
items.question: What is the chance that TTH appears first? Give four decimal places.

widget.accept: 1/4: TTH wins only when the first two flips are TT.
widget.label: Chance

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what must come just before the first TT.

byKey.even: You gave the patterns an even chance because they use the same letters. Overlaps decide the race.
byKey.other: That is the chance HTT wins. The question asks for TTH.
byKey.odds: You gave the odds, 1 to 3, as a chance. The chance is 1/(1 + 3).

explain.text: TTH needs a TT first, and a first TT that follows an H completes HTT at once. So TTH wins only if the first two flips are TT, with chance 1/4. After that start, the next H finishes TTH before HTT can form.

items.prose: A bet pays 5 to 2: each £2 staked wins £5 profit, or is lost. It wins with chance 0.35. You size each stake by the Kelly rule.
items.question: What fraction of your bankroll do you stake? Give two decimal places.

widget.accept: $f^* = 0.35 - 0.65/2.5 = 0.09$. The edge is positive, so it is a bet.
widget.label: Fraction staked

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $f^* = p - q/b$, with b the profit per £1 staked.

byKey.even-money: You used $p - q$, the rule for even money. At 5 to 2 a win pays 2.5 times the stake.
byKey.win-chance: You staked the win chance. That over-bets badly and shrinks the bankroll in the long run.
byKey.edge: That is the edge per £1, $0.35 \times 2.5 - 0.65$. Kelly divides the edge by the odds, 2.5.

explain.text: Per £1 staked a win pays $b = 2.5$, so the edge is $0.35 \times 2.5 - 0.65 = 0.225$, positive: it is a bet. Kelly stakes the edge over the odds: $f^* = 0.225/2.5 = 0.09$. The rule $p - q/b = 0.35 - 0.26$ agrees.

items.prose: You hold a position that makes £6 or loses £4, each with chance 1/2. You can close it now for a sure £0.50. You judge by the log rule from Kelly: keep the choice with the higher expected log of your bankroll.
items.question: When does closing for £0.50 beat holding?

options.text: When your bankroll is below about £24
Never, since holding is worth £1 on average
options.why: You compared expected values only. Under the log rule a £4 loss hurts a small bankroll more than £6 helps.

options.text: Always, since a sure profit beats a risky one
options.why: You ignored the cost. Closing gives up £0.50 of expected profit, and a large bankroll should keep it.

options.text: When your bankroll is above about £24
options.why: You reversed the rule. Risk matters more when the bankroll is small, so small bankrolls close.

feedback.correct: Correct. Close below £24.25 and hold above it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For a bankroll W, compare $(W + 6)(W - 4)$ with $(W + 0.5)^2$.

explain.text: Holding wins when $\tfrac12\ln(W + 6) + \tfrac12\ln(W - 4) > \ln(W + 0.5)$, that is when $(W + 6)(W - 4) > (W + 0.5)^2$. That reads $W^2 + 2W - 24 > W^2 + W + 0.25$, so $W > 24.25$. Below £24.25 the costly hedge pays: at £20 holding is worth only a sure £0.40.

items.prose: You bet £1 on a game you win with chance 0.48, paid at evens. After each loss you double the stake. You stop after a win, or after losing a £16 stake.
items.question: What is the chance a cycle ends with the £16 stake lost? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the stakes up to £16, then multiply the loss chances.

byKey.four-bets: You stopped at the £8 stake. The £16 stake is a fifth bet, so the run has five losses.
byKey.fair-coin: You used a fair coin. Each bet loses with chance 0.52, not 0.5.
byKey.six-bets: You counted a sixth bet. Stakes of £1, £2, £4, £8 and £16 make five bets.

explain.text: The stakes run £1, £2, £4, £8 and £16, so a failed cycle is five losses in a row. Each loses with chance 0.52, so the chance is $0.52^5 \approx 0.0380$. A failed cycle loses £31 against the £1 a good cycle makes.

items.prose: A chord of a unit circle is drawn by picking its midpoint uniformly at random from the whole disc.
items.question: What is the chance the chord is longer than the radius, 1? Give four decimal places.

widget.accept: 3/4: the midpoint must lie within $\sqrt3/2$ of the centre.
widget.label: Chance

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find how far from the centre the midpoint may sit, then compare areas.

byKey.endpoints: That is the answer when the two endpoints are random. Here the midpoint is uniform over the disc, a different procedure.
byKey.radius-point: You made the distance from the centre uniform. A uniform point in the disc lies far out more often, so square the distance.
byKey.shorter: That is the chance the chord is shorter than the radius. Take the complement.

explain.text: A chord at distance d from the centre has length $2\sqrt{1 - d^2}$, which beats 1 when $d < \sqrt3/2$. A uniform midpoint lands in that inner disc with chance its area share, $(\sqrt3/2)^2 = 3/4$. Other ways of drawing a chord give 2/3 or 0.866.

items.prose: Two shops open at independent uniform points along a 3 km road.
items.question: What is the expected square of the distance between them, in square kilometres?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the squared gap as $X^2 - 2XY + Y^2$ and take expectations.

byKey.distance: That is the expected distance, 3/3 = 1 km. The squared distance averages more than $1^2$.
byKey.unit-road: You used a road of length 1. On a 3 km road squared distances grow by $3^2 = 9$.
byKey.scaled-once: You scaled by 3 only. Squared distances scale by $3^2$.

explain.text: $E[(X - Y)^2] = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y)$, because the two means cancel. Each uniform on [0, 3] has variance $3^2/12 = 0.75$. So the answer is $0.75 + 0.75 = 1.5$ km².

items.prose: A needle 3 cm long falls at random on a floor ruled with parallel lines 5 cm apart.
items.question: What is the chance the needle crosses a line? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Draw the angle and the centre's distance to the nearest line as a rectangle.

byKey.ratio: You divided the needle by the gap. That holds only for a needle at right angles to the lines, so average over the angle.
byKey.full-gap: You dropped the factor 2. The centre lies within 2.5 cm of its nearest line, not 5 cm.
byKey.whole-needle: You compared the distance with the whole needle, $3\sin\theta$. Only half the needle reaches towards the nearest line.

explain.text: The centre's distance to the nearest line is uniform on [0, 2.5], and the angle uniform on $[0, \pi/2]$. The needle crosses when the distance is below $1.5\sin\theta$, a region of area 1.5 in a rectangle of area $1.25\pi$. So the chance is $1.5/(1.25\pi) = 6/(5\pi) \approx 0.3820$.
